input: Phase equilibrium is a foundational concept in separation processes, and it becomes particularly interesting when two liquids are only partially miscible with one another. When such a liquid pair is mixed together, it does not necessarily form a single homogeneous phase; instead, over a certain range of compositions, it separates into two distinct liquid phases, each containing both components but in different proportions. At the heart of this behaviour lies a single unifying condition: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of every component must be exactly the same in both phases. This elegant criterion explains why the distribution of each component between the phases settles at a particular point: any imbalance in chemical potential drives transfer of that component from one phase to the other, and transfer continues until the imbalance disappears. Once this condition is satisfied, the compositions of the two phases become fixed at a given temperature and pressure, regardless of the relative amounts of the phases present. Depending on the overall composition of the mixture, the system may contain both phases in varying proportions, or it may fall outside the two-phase region altogether and exist as a single, fully miscible phase. Furthermore, temperature exerts a strong influence on this behaviour, typically narrowing or widening the composition range over which separation occurs. Overall, the equality of chemical potential provides a powerful and general framework for understanding not only liquid-liquid equilibrium, but phase equilibrium in all of its many forms. It is also worth noting that the proportions of the two phases, as distinct from their compositions, are governed by the overall composition of the mixture as charged: the closer the overall composition lies to the composition of one of the phases, the greater the proportion of that phase in the mixture as a whole. What matters for the practitioner is that the existence of the two phases, their compositions, and their proportions are all fixed once the temperature, the pressure, and the overall charge have been specified, leaving the system no freedom to adopt any other state at equilibrium.
target: Two liquids that are only partly miscible form, over a range of overall compositions, two liquid phases in equilibrium. The equilibrium condition is stated in words first: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is equal in the two phases. A component passes between the phases while its chemical potential differs on the two sides, and the transfer runs in the direction that lowers the difference. Transfer stops when the chemical potentials match, and the phase compositions then stop changing. The compositions of the two phases are fixed by the temperature and the pressure. At a stated temperature and pressure, each phase has its own composition, and the two compositions mark the ends of the range over which the pair separates. An overall composition between the two phase compositions gives both phases, in proportions set by where the overall composition falls between them: nearer one end, that phase is the larger share of the mixture. An overall composition outside the range gives a single phase, in which the pair is fully miscible at that composition. Equality of chemical potential is the condition behind the other phase equilibria as well; a vapour in equilibrium with a liquid meets the same condition, with the phases and the components changed. The condition is a statement about the phases at equilibrium, not about the path by which equilibrium is reached. A mixture reaches the condition by transfer between the phases, and the rate of that transfer, set by mixing and by the area between the phases, is a separate matter. Temperature moves the boundary compositions, and for many pairs the two phases grow more alike as temperature rises, until above a critical solution temperature the pair is miscible in all proportions.
